public_rationale: He says ChatGPT grew because of media hype, not because it was useful or able to do anything in particular. Media attention likely helped people try it. But independent Pew surveys from the period show growth tied to concrete use. The share of employed US adults using ChatGPT for work rose 20 points in two years to 28% by early 2025. Among workers who used AI chatbots for work, 40% called them extremely or very helpful for doing things faster. Steady, task-based growth years after launch, with many users reporting real benefit, counts against the claim that usefulness played no part. Most Americans had still not used it by 2025, so hype did not 'guarantee' everyone tried it.
limitations: A causal claim: the evidence shows usefulness contributed but cannot measure hype's share.
The helpfulness figures cover AI chatbots generally, and only 40% of worker-users rated them highly, so many users were not convinced.
Scoring depends on reading 'didn't grow because it was useful' as excluding usefulness as a driver.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: ChatGPT grew because of nonstop media hype, not because it was useful, and OpenAI still can't explain what it's for.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: ChatGPT's growth from launch to May 2025 came from media hype rather than from people finding it useful for particular tasks. Usefulness played essentially no part.

Testable implication: if usefulness played no part, users would not report using it for concrete tasks at growing rates, or finding it helpful. Independent surveys during the period that show growing task-based use and reported helpfulness count against the claim.
Media attention plausibly drove awareness and trial. That alone does not support the claim, because the claim excludes usefulness, not just credits hype.
The 'company can't explain' clause is treated as rhetorical emphasis. The scoring rests on the growth-cause clause.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence from the period that ChatGPT use was mostly one-off trial, with few users doing concrete tasks or finding it helpful. Or evidence that growth tracked media coverage while task-based use did not grow.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Independent evidence from the period that growing shares of people used ChatGPT for specific tasks (work, learning) and that a substantial share of users found it helpful. That would show usefulness contributed to its growth.

evidence.excerpt: In two years, the share of employed adults who say they use ChatGPT for work has risen by 20 percentage points to 28%.
evidence.locator: section 'How have Americans used ChatGPT?', paragraph 2
evidence.explanation: Growth in ChatGPT use continued years after launch and was concentrated in concrete tasks such as work. That is hard to square with growth owing nothing to usefulness.

evidence.excerpt: Among workers who have used AI chatbots for work, 40% say these tools have been extremely or very helpful in allowing them to do things more quickly.
evidence.locator: section 'Do workers find AI chatbots helpful for their work?', paragraph 1
evidence.explanation: A substantial minority of workers who use chatbots, ChatGPT among them, report they are highly helpful. That contradicts the claim that the product was not useful or 'able to do anything in particular'. It covers AI chatbots generally, not ChatGPT alone.

evidence.excerpt: Still, 66% of Americans have not used the chatbot, including 20% who say they’ve heard nothing about it.
evidence.explanation: Despite heavy media coverage, most US adults had not used it. This tempers the idea that hype guaranteed 'everybody would try it'.

evidence.excerpt: Three-quarters of conversations focus on practical guidance, seeking information, and writing
evidence.locator: section 'What they’re using it for', paragraph 1
evidence.explanation: OpenAI's own analysis says most use is for concrete tasks, and it publicly describes what ChatGPT is used for. A company source covering data past the period; context only.
